memberDetails.id: UKBB:Pulse wave peak to peak time
memberDetails.name: Pulse wave peak to peak time
memberDetails.text:
peak to peak time in milliseconds

A digital volume pulse can be considered to be the summation of a direct and a reflected component. The direct component is due to transmission of a pressure wave from the left ventricle to the finger via the most direct route. The reflected component is formed by pressure transmitted from the heart to the lower body where it is reflected back up the aorta and thence to the finger. peak to peak time is the difference between the peak values of direct and reflected components.

memberDetails.id: UKBB:Pulse wave pressure versus time response curve
memberDetails.name: Pulse wave pressure versus time response curve
memberDetails.text:
Wave data containing 3 waveforms, each consisting of one direct and one reflected component.

A digital volume pulse can be considered to be the summation of a direct and a reflected component. The direct component is due to transmission of a pressure wave from the left ventricle to the finger via the most direct route. The reflected component is formed by pressure transmitted from the heart to the lower body where it is reflected back up the aorta and thence to the finger. Each waveform is actually a single pulse with 100 points. Since the heart rate is in beats per minute, a single beat takes 60seconds / Heart Rate and time between two beats is (60/Heart Rate)/100.

The data is formatted as follows:

  • The first number (i.e. digits before the first '|' character)indicate the number of points X,Y for the curve.
  • Each pair of X,Y values is separated by a '|' character from the preceding/succeeding pair.
  • Each pair of X,Y values is separated internally by a ',' character.
The X-axis is the time in milliseconds and the Y-axis is the Pulse signal strength in arbitrary units.

memberDetails.name: Pulse wave reflection index
memberDetails.text:
reflection index is a measure of reflection

The direct component is due to transmission of a pressure wave from the left ventricle to the finger via the most direct route. The reflected component is formed by pressure transmitted from the heart to the lower body where it is reflected back up the aorta and thence to the finger. if 'b' is the height of direct wave peak and 'a' is the height of reflected wave peak the reflected index = (a/b) * 100%

records.concept: Number of servings of a specific food item consumed (dietary recall/food frequency), categorical ordinal
records.idealCde: Number of servings of a specific food item consumed during a dietary recall or food frequency assessment, asked conditionally upon reported consumption of that food category. The CDE captures serving quantity for an individual food or food group (e.g., baked beans, coleslaw/salad vegetables in mayonnaise, crumble topping, fried/roast potatoes, or other beans/pulses/lentils). Question: 'How many servings of [specific food item] did you have?' Answer type: Categorical single-select ordinal representing serving count in standardized units (Serving), with values spanning fractional portions (quarter, half) through whole servings (1, 2) up to a maximum/ceiling category (3+ or 4+), encoded as discrete ordered categories (e.g., quarter=0.25, half=0.5, 1=1, 2=2, 3+=3 or more, 4+=4 or more).

gencde.title: Number of Servings of Specific Food Item Consumed (Categorical Ordinal) — Dietary Recall/Food Frequency
gencde.definition: The number of standardized servings of a specific food item or food group (e.g., baked beans, coleslaw, crumble topping, fried/roast potatoes, pulses/lentils) consumed during a single dietary recall or food frequency assessment occasion, captured as a categorical ordinal quantity including fractional portions.
gencde.questionText: How many servings of [specific food item] did you have?
relatedCdes: During the past month . . . Not counting what you just told me about (lettuce salads, white potatoes, cooked dried beans), and not counting rice, how often did you eat OTHER VEGETABLES?
About how often did you eat Margarine or butter on vegetables, including potatoes?
During the past month . . . How often did you eat COOKED DRIED BEANS, such as refried beans, baked beans, bean soup, and pork and beans?
gencde.rationale: Permissible values are reconciled from all observed answer concepts across five UKBB source fields: 'quarter' (¼, code 444 in source), 'half' (½, code 555 in source), 1, 2, 3, '3+' (code 300 in source for most items), '4+' (code 400 in source for crumble). Because some food items cap at '3+' and others at '4+', both upper-bound categories are retained in the canonical set to preserve the full observed value space; implementers should select the applicable upper bound per food item context. Fractional codes (0.25, 0.5) replace source sentinel integers (444, 555) for semantic clarity. The CDE is intended as a template/pattern element parameterized by [specific food item]; it is asked conditionally upon reported consumption of the relevant food category. Near-miss CDEs relate to food frequency (monthly) rather than within-occasion serving count and were used only to confirm non-overlap.

gencde.title: History of Retinal Vascular Occlusion (Stroke in the Eye or Eye Vessels)
gencde.definition: A binary indicator of whether an individual has a self-reported or clinically documented history of retinal vascular occlusion (commonly described as a stroke in the eye or eye vessels) in one or both eyes.
gencde.questionText: Have you ever been told by a doctor or health professional that you have had a retinal vascular occlusion (stroke in the eye or eye vessels) in one or both eyes?
relatedCdes: Physical findings of Right retinal vessels by Ophthalmoscopy
Physical findings of Left retinal vessels by Ophthalmoscopy
Optical coherence tomography (OCT) retinal thickness laterality type
gencde.rationale: Derived from a single source field (AI-READI mhoccur_rvo). The concept is a self-reported medical history item covering any laterality (one or both eyes) and any subtype of retinal vascular occlusion. The 'Prefer not to say' option (code 777) is retained as a permissible value per the source field; it is a response option, not a missing-data sentinel, and should be distinguished from true missing/unknown during analysis. Near-miss CDEs relate to ophthalmoscopic or OCT findings of retinal vessels rather than patient-reported occlusion history, confirming no existing CDE match. The concept is a component of broader visual impairment history but is catalogued here as a discrete ocular vascular event history element.

gencde.rationale: This concept is a poor-quality harmonization grouping: the source fields are semantically heterogeneous (dates, counts, binary yes/no, categorical employer continuity, free-text smoking years) and do not share a coherent single clinical concept. The ideal anchor CDE (work street address) is entirely unrelated to the source fields. The permissible values are drawn only from the categorical source fields (CLSA pension plan and employer continuity items). Numeric and date fields (smoking years, survey dates, number of jobs, occupational entry date) cannot be meaningfully represented in a single categorical permissible-value set. Confidence is very low (0.12) because this grouping conflates fundamentally different constructs and does not constitute a valid, coherent CDE. Recommend decomposing into separate CDEs per construct. records.concept: Concomitant medication dose unit of measure

cde.id: Medication prior or concomitant dose unit of measure

records.idealCde: Concomitant medication dose unit: the unit of measure corresponding to the administered dose of a concomitant medication, treatment, or therapy. Question answered: 'What is the unit of the dose recorded for this concomitant medication?' Answer type: categorical (enumerated), selecting one value from a standardized list of dose-unit options including but not limited to: percent volume per volume (% v/v), capsule, gram (g), inhalation, international dosing unit (IDU), liter per hour (L/hr), liter per minute (L/min), milligram (mg), milligram per kilogram (mg/kg), milliliter (mL), milliliter per hour (mL/hr), milliliter per kilogram (mL/kg), puff, spray.

Compound units (mg/kg, mcg/kg, mL/hr, mL/kg, L/hr, L/min) have no direct CDE equivalent. Dosage forms (Capsule, Tablet, Puff, Spray, Inhalation) are not dose units in the CDE sense. Percent Volume per Volume and International Dosing Unit also lack CDE equivalents. These could arguably be mapped to 'Other, specify' but without clear guidance they are left unmapped to avoid overreach. Extended against the refined element (REFCDE:ca5dd4fd751c3#g0): 17 of 18 source codes now map.

records.concept: Reason standing height measurement was not performed (coded categorical)
records.idealCde: Anthropometric measurement administration status and context for body size assessments (standing height, seated height, waist circumference, weight) collected at an assessment centre visit. Captures: (1) reason a specific body measurement was not performed, answered as a post-hoc coded categorical value derived from staff-entered free-text (e.g., Declined, Against participant's beliefs, Unable to perform, Technical failure, Other); (2) seated height measurement value in centimeters (continuous, cm) obtained with participant seated on a standardized box using a Seca 202 device; (3) box height used during seated height measurement as a categorical value (30 cm, 40 cm, or 50 cm). Each skip-reason element is measurement-specific (standing height, waist, weight) and should be recorded as a separate categorical single-select field per measurement type. The seated height and box-height fields are paired and apply to the seated-height procedure only. Answer types: skip-reason fields = categorical single (coded integer with labeled categories); seated height = continuous numeric (cm); box height = categorical single (30, 40, or 50 cm).

memberDetails.name: Reason for skipping standing height
memberDetails.text:
Reason standing height measurement was not performed (entered as free-text by a UK Biobank Staff member).

This field was created by post-hoc coding the free-text reasons entered during the assessment centre visit. The encoding used was constructed after the data had been examined to determine suitable representative groupings.

transforms.rationale: The CDE offers only two target codes: 'Not applicable' and 'Unknown'. 'Unknown' maps to source codes 300 ('Reason not known') and 506 ('Reason not known'), as these explicitly indicate the reason is not known. 'Not applicable' has no clear source equivalent — none of the source codes indicate the measurement is simply not applicable in a generic sense; they all describe specific reasons for non-completion (participant refusal, health issues, equipment failure, etc.) which are more granular than either CDE option supports. The vast majority of source codes cannot be confidently mapped to either CDE value without losing critical specificity, so they are listed as unmapped. Confidence is moderate-low due to the very coarse CDE value set relative to the rich source taxonomy. Extended against the refined element (REFCDE:c96bf5464788a#g0): 33 of 41 source codes now map.

Captures: (1) reason a specific body measurement was not performed, answered as a post-hoc coded categorical value derived from staff-entered free-text (e.g., Declined, Against participant's beliefs, Unable to perform, Technical failure, Other); (2) seated height measurement value in centimeters (continuous, cm) obtained with participant seated on a standardized box using a Seca 202 device; (3) box height used during seated height measurement as a categorical value (30 cm, 40 cm, or 50 cm). Each skip-reason element is measurement-specific (standing height, waist, weight) and should be recorded as a separate categorical single-select field per measurement type. The seated height and box-height fields are paired and apply to the seated-height procedure only. Answer types: skip-reason fields = categorical single (coded integer with labeled categories); seated height = continuous numeric (cm); box height = categorical single (30, 40, or 50 cm).

memberDetails.name: Reason for skipping weight
memberDetails.text:
Reason weight measurement was not performed (entered as free-text by a UK Biobank Staff member).

This field was created by post-hoc coding the free-text reasons entered during the assessment centre visit. The encoding used was constructed after the data had been examined to determine suitable representative groupings.

transforms.rationale: The CDE offers only two target codes: 'Not applicable' and 'Unknown'. 'Unknown' maps to source codes 300 ('Reason not known') and 506 ('Reason not known'), as these explicitly indicate the reason is not known. 'Not applicable' has no clear source equivalent — none of the source codes indicate the measurement is simply not applicable in a generic sense; they all describe specific reasons for non-completion (participant refusal, health issues, equipment failure, etc.) which are more granular than either CDE option supports. The vast majority of source codes cannot be confidently mapped to either CDE value without losing critical specificity, so they are listed as unmapped. Confidence is moderate-low due to the very coarse CDE value set relative to the rich source taxonomy. Extended against the refined element (REFCDE:c96bf5464788a#g2): 41 of 41 source codes now map.

records.concept: Age category at first diagnosis of bacterial STI (Gonorrhea, Syphilis, Chlamydia)
records.idealCde: Sexually Transmitted Infections (STI) — Bacterial (Gonorrhea, Syphilis, Chlamydia) — Age at First Diagnosis and Current Treatment Status: A pair of CDEs capturing (1) the self-reported age category at which the respondent was first told by a healthcare provider that they had a bacterial STI (gonorrhea, syphilis, or chlamydia), answered as an ordinal categorical variable with mutually exclusive age-range bands: Child (0–11), Adolescent (12–17), Adult (18–64), Older Adult (65–74), Elderly (75+); and (2) whether the respondent is currently prescribed medication and/or receiving treatment for a bacterial STI (gonorrhea, syphilis, or chlamydia), answered as a binary Yes/No. Both questions are self-reported, refer to the respondent themselves, and pertain to the specific STI cluster of gonorrhea, syphilis, and chlamydia.

gencde.rationale: Derived from a single AoU source field (infectiousdiseases_howoldwereyoustis) using a radio-button ordinal scale. The five age-band categories (Child 0–11, Adolescent 12–17, Adult 18–64, Older Adult 65–74, Elderly 75+) are directly preserved from the source without modification. Near-miss CDEs for NHL exposure age and other STD type text were used only to confirm non-overlap and inform alias labeling. Confidence is high given unambiguous single-source mapping and clean, non-overlapping ordinal bands; slight reduction from 1.0 reflects the absence of corroborating multi-cohort sources.

records.concept: Sexual history section navigation consent/preference gate question (continue vs skip entire section)
records.idealCde: Sexual history section navigation consent/preference: A gate question presented before a sensitive sexual history questionnaire section, asking whether the participant wishes to continue with the section or skip it entirely. Answer type: categorical single-select; values: Continue (proceed to sexual history questions) | Skip this section (bypass entire sexual history section).

gencde.title: Sexual History Section Navigation Consent/Preference Gate
gencde.definition: A gate question presented immediately before a sensitive sexual history questionnaire section that asks the participant whether they wish to proceed with the section or bypass it entirely, enabling informed voluntary participation in sensitive data collection.
gencde.questionText: The next section contains questions about your sexual history. If you feel that a question is too sensitive, you can skip the question or skip the entire section if you prefer. Would you like to continue or skip this section?
relatedCdes: How much does your spouse or partner really care about you [MIDUS II]
Other than what we just talked about, has anyone ever actually touched private parts of your body or made you touch theirs against your wishes [LTVH]
Score for question 4 indicating if the subject belongs to any clubs or organizations
gencde.rationale: Concept is well-defined and sourced from a single cohort (UK Biobank ACE touchscreen), yielding high confidence in the permissible-value set. The two observed answer concepts (Continue, Skip this section) are unambiguous and require no synonym merging. This element functions as a routing/branching gate rather than a clinical measurement; it captures participant preference/consent to engage with sensitive sexual history content. Near-miss CDEs were confirmed non-matching (different constructs: partner care, unwanted touching, club membership). No numeric or date domain is applicable.

records.concept: Weekly frequency of eating regular (non-low-fat) snack chips or crackers
records.idealCde: Dietary fat and sugar intake frequency: A self-reported dietary behavior assessment capturing how often an individual consumes high-fat and high-sugar foods and beverages, including regular (non-low-fat) snack chips/crackers, desserts/sweets, added fats (butter, margarine, or meat fat used as seasoning or spread), and fruit juice. The CDE answers: 'How frequently do you consume specific high-fat or high-sugar food items?' Answer type: ordinal frequency scale per item, with response options ranging across consumption frequency categories (e.g., rarely/never, less than once per week, 1 time or less per week, 2–3 times per week, 4 or more times per week, per day/week/month/year as applicable), plus a 'Prefer not to say' option; administered as a multi-item self-report questionnaire with one ordinal response per food/beverage category. No laterality, body site, or specific subject qualifier is specified beyond self-report.

gencde.title: Weekly Frequency of Eating Regular (Non-Low-Fat) Snack Chips or Crackers
gencde.definition: Self-reported number of times per week an individual consumed regular (non-low-fat) snack chips or crackers, captured as an ordinal frequency category.
gencde.questionText: How many times a week did you eat regular snack chips or crackers (not low-fat)?
relatedCdes: About how often did you eat Sausage or bacon, regular-fat?
About how often did you eat Cold cereal?
About how often did you eat French fries, home fries, or hash brown potatoes?
gencde.rationale: Single source field (AI-READI:diet6) with a clear ordinal weekly frequency scale. Code 777 (Prefer not to say) is retained as a permissible value per source data rather than treated as a missing-data sentinel, consistent with the source field design. Near-miss CDEs for sausage/bacon, cold cereal, and French fries confirm this concept belongs to a broader dietary fat/snack food frequency domain but is distinct in food item specificity. No additional answer concepts were introduced beyond those observed in the source field.

gencde.rationale: The two source fields use fundamentally different response scales: AI-READI uses an amount-based ordinal scale (Very little, Some, A lot) while CLSA uses a time-frequency scale (Rarely/Never, Per Day, Per Week, Per Month, Per Year). These scales are not directly reconcilable into a single clean ordinal set without losing measurement fidelity. The permissible values above represent a pragmatic merge that preserves all observed answer concepts, but analysts should be aware that codes 0–2 conflate amount and frequency concepts across cohorts. Harmonization is approximate; cohort-specific mappings should be documented. The 'Prefer not to say' sentinel (code 777) is retained as a response option rather than a missing-data sentinel since it represents a deliberate participant choice. Near-miss CDEs (NHANES-style butter/margarine frequency items) were used only to inform aliases.

Because they share the same data type, unit convention, and measurement construct (continuous dietary intake score per vegetable subgroup), they are harmonized into a single CDE with a subcategory qualifier. The ideal CDE anchor described fat/sugar intake, which is unrelated; it was disregarded for content but noted as a mismatch. Near-miss CDEs (salad frequency, PhenX fresh fruit/vegetable quality, food hypersensitivity) were used only to inform aliases. No upper bound is specified as maximum scores depend on FFQ design and portion-size assumptions. Units are expressed as servings per day, consistent with standard MESA food group scoring conventions.

gencde.title: Breakfast Cereal Dried Fruit Content Indicator
gencde.definition: A self-reported indicator of whether the breakfast cereal consumed by an individual on the previous day contained dried fruit (e.g., sultanas, raisins, or other dried fruit inclusions).

gencde.rationale: Source field is from UK Biobank 24-hour dietary recall (Oxford WebQ), asked only of participants who reported eating breakfast cereal the previous day. Only two answer concepts were observed across source fields: 'Yes' (code 1) and 'Varied' (code 2, indicating the cereal type varied and thus dried fruit content was inconsistent). A 'No' response option was presumably available in the instrument but was not represented in the pooled answer concepts provided, so it is excluded per instructions. The near-miss CDEs relate to cereal type frequency or general fruit intake and are distinct from this binary/categorical dried-fruit-in-cereal indicator. Confidence is moderate due to single-cohort sourcing and the absence of a 'No' permissible value in the observed data.

gencde.title: Major Dietary Changes in the Last 5 Years and Reason
gencde.definition: A self-reported indicator of whether a participant has made any major changes to their diet in the past 5 years, and if so, the primary reason for those changes (illness-related or other reasons).

relatedCdes: Dietary recommendation indicator
Dietary intervention type
Overall diet health scale
gencde.rationale: Sourced exclusively from UK Biobank (UKBB) ACE touchscreen field. The 'Prefer not to answer' sentinel value (-3) was excluded from the canonical permissible-value set per harmonization instructions. Three substantive answer concepts are retained: no change, change due to illness, and change due to other reasons. Near-miss CDEs (Dietary recommendation indicator, Dietary intervention type, Overall diet health scale) informed alias selection but were not matched because this concept specifically captures self-reported dietary change occurrence and reason over a defined 5-year lookback window, rather than dietary quality, recommendations, or intervention type per se.

gencde.title: Reason Participant Did Not Eat or Drink Normally on Dietary Recall Day
gencde.definition: The self-reported reason(s) why a participant did not eat or drink in their usual manner on the day prior to a dietary recall assessment, captured as one or more categorical responses indicating illness, fasting, being away from home, or another unspecified atypical dietary circumstance.

gencde.rationale: Source field is from UK Biobank (UKBB) dietary recall module; original codes 3–6 were remapped to sequential codes 1–4 to remove non-semantic gaps. The field supports multiple simultaneous selections (categorical multiple), so implementations should allow multi-select. Codes align with the four Yes/No sub-questions asked when a participant reports atypical intake. Near-miss CDEs (PhenX fasting screen, mitochondrial disease diet reason) were consulted for alias terminology only and do not share the same permissible-value structure. The ideal CDE anchor provided (dietary fat/sugar frequency) is conceptually unrelated and was used solely to confirm non-overlap.

Answer type: ordinal frequency scale per item, with response options ranging across consumption frequency categories (e.g., rarely/never, less than once per week, 1 time or less per week, 2–3 times per week, 4 or more times per week, per day/week/month/year as applicable), plus a 'Prefer not to say' option; administered as a multi-item self-report questionnaire with one ordinal response per food/beverage category. No laterality, body site, or specific subject qualifier is specified beyond self-report.

gencde.rationale: Two UKBB source fields were reconciled: the main touchscreen used Never/rarely, Sometimes, Often; the pilot version used Never/rarely, Sometimes, Usually, Always. All five observed labels are retained in a single canonical ordinal sequence (1–5). 'Often' and 'Usually' are treated as distinct ordinal steps rather than synonyms because both appear in the pooled source data and occupy different positions in their respective scales. Missing-data sentinels (-1=Do not know, -3=Prefer not to answer) are excluded per instructions. The near-miss CDEs (hearing day-to-day variation, special diet reason, fat intake frequency) informed alias vocabulary but were not merged into this element, as the concept is specifically about temporal consistency of overall diet rather than dietary content or a different sensory modality.

gencde.rationale: The single source field (CLSA NUR_SWLLFD_MCQ) uses a free-text type annotation but the question stem and CLSA documentation indicate a standard 5-point frequency response scale (Never–Always); permissible values are reconstructed from the canonical CLSA response set and corroborated by analogous SWAL-QOL frequency items. Near-miss CDEs (SWAL-QOL choking indicator, regurgitation frequency) were used only to confirm aliases and scope boundaries; they differ in symptom specificity or instrument context. Confidence is moderate (0.72) because the source field's declared type is 'text' and no explicit coded value list was provided in the harmonization metadata, requiring inference from the question stem and instrument documentation.

records.concept: Currently prescribed medications and/or receiving treatment for anemia (Yes/No)
records.idealCde: This source concept groups heterogeneous fields that do NOT measure the same construct and should not be harmonized into a single CDE. The member fields span at least two distinct domains: (1) current prescription medication or treatment status for a specific circulatory/hematologic condition (anemia; bleeding disorder) — a binary Yes/No clinical treatment indicator per named condition — and (2) frequency of adding table salt to food, an ordinal dietary behavior measure (0=Does not eat the food, 1=Seldom or never, 2=Sometimes, 3=Often or always). If a single CDE must be described, the dominant structured construct is: Current treatment status for a named hematologic condition — 'Are you currently prescribed medications and/or receiving treatment for [specified condition: anemia / bleeding disorder]?' — answered as a binary categorical (Yes / No), with the condition name carried as a required qualifier. The dietary salt-addition field is a separate CDE: frequency of adding table salt to food at the table or during preparation, answered on a 4-point ordinal frequency scale (0=Does not eat the food, 1=Seldom or never, 2=Sometimes, 3=Often or always). These represent distinct CDEs and should not be merged.

The IDEAL CDE note flags heterogeneity in the broader harmonization group (which also included a dietary salt frequency measure), but the dominant and well-defined construct here is a binary clinical treatment indicator for anemia. Permissible values are collapsed from the source labels (RxMedsforAnemia_Yes → Yes, RxMedsforAnemia_No → No) with clean sequential binary codes. Near-miss CDEs (iron chelation treatment, sickle cell transfusion) are related but narrower in scope and were not matched. records.idealCde: Current mental health and substance use treatment status: A set of condition-specific items assessing whether an individual is currently receiving medical care or pharmacological treatment for discrete mental health and substance use conditions. Each item asks a yes/no question about a named condition (e.g., depression, alcohol use disorder, other mental health/substance use condition) or a specific treatment behavior (e.g., use of sleeping pills in the past 2 weeks, prescription medications for alcohol use disorder). Answer type: categorical/radio per item — sleeping pill use frequency captured on a 5-point ordinal scale (No / Every day / Most days [3–4 days/week] / Some days [1–2 days/week] / A few days [<1 day/week]) with 'Don't know/not sure' and 'Decline to answer' options; current provider-care and prescription-treatment items captured as binary Yes/No. Subject qualifier: self-report. Time window qualifier: current (ongoing care) or past 2 weeks (sleeping pill use). Conditions covered span depression, alcohol use disorder, and other mental health or substance use conditions.

gencde.rationale: Permissible values are derived exclusively from the AI-READI cm_slp source field. Codes were reassigned sequentially (0–4) in ascending frequency order, with missing-data sentinels (Don't know/not sure, Decline to answer) assigned conventional codes 99 and 77 respectively. The original source code '2' (A few days) was renumbered to '1' and codes shifted accordingly to reflect a logical ordinal progression from no use to daily use. Near-miss CDEs address sleep difficulty (PROMIS) and testosterone use, which are conceptually distinct; no aliases were borrowed from those elements. The concept aligns with PHQ-adjacent sleep pharmacotherapy screening items and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index sleep medication subscale in spirit, though it is not a direct match to either.

gencde.rationale: Source field is from the All of Us (AoU) COPE survey (tsu_ds5_13_xx34), using COPE answer codes A_227–A_229. The three permissible values are ordinal and directional (less/same/more), reflecting change relative to the respondent's own baseline rather than an absolute frequency. No missing-data sentinel codes were present in the source. Codes assigned sequentially in ascending order of use frequency change.

records.concept: More breathless walking up hills or steps (binary Yes/No/Unknown)
records.idealCde: Exertional dyspnea symptom assessment: captures whether the respondent experiences increased breathlessness during physical exertion, assessed separately for two activity contexts — (1) walking up hills or steps and (2) walking on level ground. Each item answers the question 'Are you more breathless when [activity]?' Expected answer type: categorical binary per item (No / Yes), with provision for an unknown/unable-to-answer response; coded as numeric (0=No, 1=Yes, 9=Do Not Know/Unknown). No laterality or body-site qualifier; qualifier is the specific exertional context (incline vs. level ground).

gencde.title: More Breathless Walking Up Hills or Steps
gencde.definition: A binary self-report item indicating whether the respondent experiences increased breathlessness (dyspnea) specifically during the exertional activity of walking up hills or steps, compared to level-ground walking.

records.concept: Ever addicted to or dependent on prescription or over-the-counter medication
records.idealCde: Prescription or over-the-counter medication addiction or dependence history (conditional on prior affirmative response to medication use/exposure): captures whether the respondent has ever been addicted to or dependent on prescription or over-the-counter medication. Question: 'Have you been addicted to or dependent on prescription or over-the-counter medication?' Answer type: categorical single-select; permissible values: Yes | No | Do not know | Prefer not to answer.

gencde.title: Ever Addicted to or Dependent on Prescription or Over-the-Counter Medication
gencde.definition: Indicates whether the respondent has ever been addicted to or dependent on any prescription or over-the-counter medication, assessed among individuals who have previously reported medication use or exposure.

relatedCdes: Medication over the counter indicator
Substance Abuse Prescription Illicit Substance Over the Counter Product Personal Medical History Yes No Indicator

gencde.rationale: Source field (UKBB) included four response options (-818=Prefer not to answer, -121=Do not know, 0=No, 1=Yes), but the ANSWER CONCEPTS observed and reconciled across cohorts reduce to only Yes and No; missing-data sentinels (Prefer not to answer, Do not know) are excluded per instructions. Data type is set to binary rather than categorical because only two substantive answer concepts are present. The question is conditional on a prior affirmative response to a medication use/exposure screener (UKBB field ~F20401~). Near-miss CDEs confirm adjacency to OTC and prescription medication indicator concepts but none capture the addiction/dependence lifetime history dimension.

records.concept: Visual acuity letter score and LogMAR under mesopic and photopic conditions for each eye (OD and OS)
records.idealCde: Visual acuity measured separately under two luminance conditions (mesopic low-luminance and photopic standard-luminance) for each eye individually (right eye [OD] and left eye [OS]); answers the question 'What is the patient's visual acuity under mesopic and photopic conditions for each eye?'; recorded as both a raw letter score (integer count of letters read correctly, text entry) and a derived LogMAR score (continuous calculated value in LogMAR units); qualifier: laterality (OD vs OS) and luminance condition (mesopic vs photopic) are both required dimensions of the CDE.

gencde.title: Visual Acuity Letter Score and LogMAR Under Mesopic and Photopic Conditions by Eye (OD/OS)
gencde.definition: A composite clinical measurement capturing the number of letters correctly identified (raw letter score) and the derived logarithm of the minimum angle of resolution (LogMAR) value for each eye individually (right eye [OD] and left eye [OS]) under both mesopic (low-luminance) and photopic (standard-luminance) conditions during standardized visual acuity testing.

Woodcock Johnson III (WJ-III) ? Letter-word identification correct count
CAMPHOR Overall Score
gencde.rationale: This CDE is a multi-dimensional construct requiring four sub-elements per subject: (1) mesopic letter score OD, (2) mesopic LogMAR OD, (3) photopic letter score OD, (4) photopic LogMAR OD, and the corresponding four for OS — eight values total. The letter score sub-elements are integer counts (text entry in source, treated as integer numeric); the LogMAR sub-elements are continuous calculated values (typically ranging from approximately -0.3 to 3.0 in clinical practice, but no hard maximum is imposed here). Laterality (OD vs OS) and luminance condition (mesopic vs photopic) are required qualifying dimensions. Near-miss CDEs (WJ-III letter-word identification, CAMPHOR Overall Score) were excluded as they measure literacy/quality-of-life constructs unrelated to ophthalmic acuity. No permissible-value enumeration is applicable given the continuous/integer numeric nature of both sub-element types. Source fields from AI-READI cohort (viaodmlog, viaodmscore, viaodplog, viaodpscore, viaosmlog, viaosmscore, viaosplog, viaospscore) were fully reconciled into this single CDE with laterality and luminance as mandatory qualifiers.

records.concept: Area-level income/multiple deprivation score or proportion for a small geographic area (LSOA or equivalent)
records.idealCde: Area-level income deprivation score or proportion: captures the extent of income deprivation within a small area (LSOA or equivalent), answering 'What proportion of the population in this geographic area is experiencing income deprivation (i.e., living in low-income households or claiming income-related benefits)?'. Answer type: numeric proportion or score (continuous, typically expressed as a rate between 0 and 1, or as a ranked/decile index value), attributed to a defined small-area geographic unit (e.g., LSOA in England or Wales). Derived from aggregated counts of individuals in income-deprived households across multiple benefit/low-income indicators; no individual-level qualifier — unit of analysis is the area, not a specific person.

gencde.title: Area-Level Income Deprivation Score or Proportion (Small Area / LSOA)
gencde.definition: A continuous numeric measure capturing the extent of income deprivation within a small geographic area (e.g., Lower Layer Super Output Area [LSOA] in England or Wales), expressed as a proportion of the population experiencing low income or claiming income-related benefits, or as a composite index score derived from multiple deprivation domains weighted and ranked at the small-area level.
gencde.questionText: What is the income deprivation score or index of multiple deprivation score for the small geographic area (LSOA or equivalent) in which this individual resides?
aliases: Welsh Index of Multiple Deprivation (WIMD) Score
English Indices of Deprivation Income Domain
relatedCdes: Household Member Size
Family income supported persons count
Health Disparity Outcomes (Project Level)
gencde.rationale: Source fields span two distinct but harmonizable constructs: (1) a pure income deprivation proportion (proportion of LSOA population in low-income households or claiming income-related benefits, range 0–1) from the England and Wales Income Domain scores, and (2) a composite Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) score that incorporates income as the dominant weighted domain alongside employment, health, education, housing, environment, access, and community safety. Both are continuous, small-area (LSOA-level) measures. The canonical CDE is defined as the income deprivation proportion/score (0–1 scale) to reflect the ideal CDE anchor and the majority of source fields; IMD composite scores may exceed 1.0 and are noted as a related variant. Units are expressed as a dimensionless proportion (UCUM '1'). The maximum_value of 1 applies strictly to the proportion-based fields; composite IMD scores may have different practical ranges depending on the edition and country. Near-miss CDEs (Household Member Size, Family income supported persons count, Health Disparity Outcomes) were used only to confirm non-overlap and inform alias exclusions. Confidence is modestly reduced from 1.0 because two of the four source fields are composite IMD scores rather than pure income proportions, introducing conceptual heterogeneity within the harmonized set.

memberDetails.name: Income score (England)
memberDetails.text:
This domain measures the proportion of the population in an area experiencing deprivation related to low income. A combined count of income deprived individuals per LSOA is calculated by summing the following five indicators:
  • Adults and children in Income Support families
  • Adults and children in Income-Based Jobseeker's Allowance families
  • Adults and children in Pension Credit (Guarantee) families
  • Adults and children in Child Tax Credit families (who are not in receipt of Income Support, Income-Based Jobseeker's Allowance or Pension Credit) whose equivalised income (excluding housing benefits) is below 60 per cent of the median before housing costs
  • Asylum seekers in England in receipt of subsistence support, accommodation support, or both.

memberDetails.name: Income score (Wales)
memberDetails.text:
The purpose of this domain is to capture the extent of deprivation relating to income at a small area level across Wales. It focuses on the proportion of people living in households with income below a defined threshold or claiming benefits relating to low incomes. The indicators used for the income domain were:
  • Adults & children in income support households
  • Adults & children in pension credit households
  • Adults & children in income-based job seekers allowance households
  • Adults & children in tax credit (child tax credit and working tax credit) households below a low income threshold
  • National Asylum Support Service (NASS) supported asylum seekers in Wales in receipt of subsistence only and accommodation support

memberDetails.name: Index of Multiple Deprivation (England)
memberDetails.text:
The English Indices of Deprivation 2010 are measures of multiple deprivation at the small area level. The model of multiple deprivation which underpins the Indices of Deprivation 2010 is based on the idea of distinct domains of deprivation which can be recognised and measured separately. These domains are experienced by individuals living in an area. People may be counted in one or more of the domains, depending on the number of types of deprivation that they experience.

Each domain represents a specific form of deprivation experienced by people and each can be measured individually using a number of indicators. Seven distinct domains have been identified in the English Indices of Deprivation; Income Deprivation, Employment Deprivation, Health Deprivation and Disability, Education Skills and Training Deprivation, Barriers to Housing and Services, Living Environment Deprivation, and Crime. Individual domains can be used in isolation as measures of each specific form of deprivation. They can also be combined, using appropriate weights, into a single overall Index of Multiple Deprivation which can be used to rank every small area in England according to the deprivation experienced by the people living there. Along with two supplementary indices, Income Deprivation Affecting Children Index and Income Deprivation Affecting Older People Index, they form the English Indices of Deprivation. These statistics allow the most, and least, deprived areas of the country to be identified as well as providing information about the issues faced by people living in different parts of the country.

memberDetails.name: Index of Multiple Deprivation (Wales)
memberDetails.text:
The Welsh Index of Multiple Deprivation 2008 is the official measure of deprivation for small areas in Wales. It was developed for the Welsh Assembly Government by the Assembly's Statistical Directorate and the Local Government Data Unit (Wales).

The WIMD 2008 is made up of eight separate domains (or kinds) of deprivation: income, employment, health, education, housing, environment, access to services, and community safety.

Each of them was based on a range of different indicators which meant that they were measured in different ways using different units. So before they could be combined the measurements had to be transformed to make them compatible. For example, if the height of something had been measured in metres and the weight in kilograms it would not make sense simply to add them together.

Income and employment were classed as the most important factors, and they were given the biggest weighting in the overall index. Although there is more to deprivation than poverty, not having enough money or a job is a big part of it.

records.concept: Difficulty initiating effortful activity ('getting going') — frequency over past week

cde.id: Center for Epidemiologic Studies-Depression Scale (CES-D) - get going indicator

records.idealCde: Functional limitation in independent activity execution — captures the degree to which a person experiences difficulty or inability to initiate or sustain goal-directed activity (e.g., 'getting going') and to perform errands independently (e.g., visiting a doctor's office or shopping) due to physical, mental, or emotional conditions. The CDE answers: 'To what extent does the respondent have trouble initiating effortful activity, and does a health condition prevent them from doing errands alone?' The member fields carry different qualifiers and constructs: one measures frequency of low motivation/psychomotor slowing as a depressive symptom (ordinal scale: 0=Rarely or none of the time [<1 day] to 3=All of the time [5–7 days] over the past week), and the other measures binary self-reported functional disability specifically for independent errand-running due to any physical, mental, or emotional condition (Yes / No / Prefer not to answer). Ideal answer type: ordinal frequency rating (4-point Likert, 0–3, past-week timeframe) for the motivational/initiation item; categorical yes/no (with prefer-not-to-answer option) for the functional disability/errands item. These two constructs should ideally be captured as separate CDEs but are harmonized here under the shared domain of functional and behavioral capacity limitation.

Answers the question: 'Can you walk or cycle on your own, without help from another person or a mobility aid, for 10 minutes?' Expected answer type: categorical (Yes / No / Unsure). Intended as a pre-exercise or fitness-test safety screen to establish basic unassisted ambulatory capacity.

gencde.title: Ability to Walk or Cycle Unaided for 10 Continuous Minutes (Pre-Exercise Safety Screen)
gencde.definition: A categorical pre-exercise safety screening item indicating whether the respondent is able to walk or cycle without assistive devices or personal assistance for at least 10 continuous minutes.
gencde.questionText: Are you able to walk or cycle unaided for 10 minutes?
aliases: Exercise safety screen: walking or cycling capacity
Ability to ambulate or cycle independently for 10 minutes
Unaided walking or cycling endurance screen
sourceVariables: UKBB:Able to walk or cycle unaided for 10 minutes
relatedCdes: In the past 7 days, How many days did you exercise <u>really hard</u> for 10 minutes or more?
Are you able to walk a block (about 100 m) on flat ground?
How many days did your child exercise really hard for 10 minutes or more?
gencde.rationale: Single source field (UK Biobank exercise safety question 4) with three observed answer concepts (Yes, No, Unsure) directly mapped to canonical codes 1, 0, 2 respectively, preserving original UKBB coding. Near-miss CDEs address related but distinct constructs (days of vigorous exercise, ability to walk 100 m on flat ground) and were used only to confirm non-overlap. No permissible values were added beyond those observed in the source field. Confidence slightly below 1.0 due to single-cohort provenance; broader multi-cohort validation would increase certainty.

records.concept: Driving-related topics discussed with a medical professional (multi-select: herbal supplements, medications, medical conditions/health threats)
records.idealCde: Driving-related topics discussed with a medical professional: captures which specific driving-related subjects (e.g., herbal supplements, medications, medical conditions/health threats) the respondent discussed with a medical professional in the context of their driving. Question: 'Which of the following topics related to your driving did you discuss with the medical professional?' Answer type: categorical multi-select (select all that apply), with response options representing distinct topic categories such as herbal/supplement use, prescription/OTC medication use, and medical conditions or health threats affecting driving; each topic captured as a separate binary or multi-choice text field.

gencde.rationale: Three CLSA source fields (HRB = herbal supplements, MED = medications, THR = threats/medical conditions) each carry the same question stem but capture a distinct topic category via separate multi-select checkbox variables; they are reconciled here into a single canonical permissible-value set with codes 1–3. Response format is select-all-that-apply (multi-select categorical). Near-miss CDEs (current driving status, drowsy driving, night driving difficulty) are related but measure different constructs and were used only to confirm non-overlap and inform alias terminology. No missing-data sentinels were included per instructions.

records.idealCde: Depression symptom frequency during a defined reference term/period: ordinal self-report item asking how often the respondent experienced a specified depressive symptom (e.g., feeling depressed; feeling fearful or tearful) within the past week or study term. Question: 'How often did you feel [symptom] during the past [term/week]?' Answer type: 4-point ordinal frequency scale — 1=All of the time (5–7 days), 2=Occasionally (3–4 days), 3=Some of the time (1–2 days), 4=Rarely or never (less than 1 day). Qualifier: symptom-specific item within a depression symptom frequency battery, referenced to a defined study term/time window (trm).

records.concept: Diabetes diagnosis type (Type I / Type II / Neither)
records.idealCde: Age or year at first occurrence of a diagnosed condition (cancer, non-cancer illness, or surgical operation): captures the timing of initial diagnosis or procedure onset as reported by the participant or recorded by a nurse via pop-up entry. Question: 'What was your age or the year when this condition/cancer/operation was first diagnosed or performed?' Answer type: Integer representing either age in years or calendar year of first occurrence; coded values include -1 = Time uncertain/unknown and -3 = Preferred not to answer. Applicable across condition categories (malignant neoplasm, non-cancer illness, surgical operation); the specific condition type and diagnosis (e.g., diabetes Type I, Type II, or Neither) should be captured in a companion classification field.

gencde.title: Diabetes Diagnosis Type (Type I / Type II / Neither)

gencde.rationale: Derived from a single CLSA source field (DIA_TYPE_COM). The three permissible values (Type I, Type II, Neither) are mapped directly from observed answer concepts with no additions. 'Neither' serves as the negative/absence category rather than a missing-data sentinel. Near-miss CDEs (COVID-19 diagnosis date, autoimmune disease PhenX, diagnosis age type) were used only to confirm non-overlap and inform alias labeling. Confidence is high given unambiguous concept and clean value set, with minor deduction for single-cohort sourcing.

relatedCdes: Usual headache treatment PhenX
Additional medications freq PhenX
Medications Current medication [PhenX]
gencde.rationale: Derived from a single MESA source field (gout5c) with a clean binary 0/1 encoding. The canonical permissible-value set collapses to No=0 and Yes=1, consistent with the observed answer concepts. Near-miss CDEs (PhenX headache treatment, additional medications frequency, current medications) address general or non-gout-specific medication use and were excluded as matches. Aliases reference standard clinical terminology for gout pharmacotherapy (e.g., urate-lowering therapy) to support cross-study discovery. Confidence is slightly below 1.0 because only one source cohort contributed, limiting cross-cohort validation of the value domain.

transforms.rationale: The source variable captures whether a respondent takes medication for Stroke, so 'Yes' maps to the CDE value 'Stroke'. The 'No' response indicates absence of the condition/treatment and has no corresponding CDE code to map to (the CDE lists conditions, not negations). Extended against the refined element (REFCDE:c68a888299a6f#g0): 2 of 2 source codes now map.

The source variable captures whether a respondent takes prescription medications for acid reflux (GERD/gastroesophageal reflux disease). This condition does not map to any specific CDE permissible value. It could loosely fall under 'Other chronic diseases/specify', but since the source codes are Yes/No responses to a single condition question rather than condition labels themselves, and acid reflux is not explicitly listed in the CDE, no confident mapping is possible. Both source codes are left unmapped.

The source variable captures whether a participant takes prescription medications for Celiac Disease, which is a binary Yes/No response. The TARGET CDE lists specific health conditions (not Yes/No responses), so there is no structural alignment. Celiac Disease itself does not appear in the CDE's value set, and the closest candidate ('Autoimmune/Immunocompromised condition') is not a confident match without explicit guidance. The Yes/No codes cannot be mapped to any CDE condition code. Both source codes are left unmapped.

The source variable captures whether a patient takes medications for colon polyps (Yes/No). This is a binary treatment indicator, not a disease/condition category. Colon polyps could potentially fall under 'Cancer' or 'Other chronic diseases/specify', but the source codes represent Yes/No responses to a treatment question, not condition labels. There is no meaningful direct mapping to any specific CDE condition code. Both source codes are unmapped.

The source variable 'RxMedsforChronicLungDisease_Yes' indicates the respondent takes prescription medications for chronic lung disease, which aligns with the CDE category for Other Chronic Respiratory Disease (e.g., COPD, Emphysema). The 'No' response indicates absence of this condition/treatment and maps to no CDE condition code (it would correspond to 'None of the above' only in a broader context, but since this is a single-condition variable rather than a multi-select list, it is left unmapped). Confidence is moderate because 'chronic lung disease' could also include Asthma, which has its own CDE code, but without further specificity the broader respiratory category is the best fit.

The source variable is a binary YES/NO indicator (1=YES, 0=NO), likely a flag for whether a condition applies, rather than a categorical condition type. It does not correspond to any specific named condition in the CDE value set. Without knowing which condition this YES/NO refers to, no meaningful mapping to CDE condition codes is possible. Both source codes are unmapped.

The source variable is a binary Yes/No response (1=Yes, 2=No), which does not correspond to any specific condition in the CDE's list of health conditions. The source codes cannot be mapped to any CDE target codes because they represent a different data structure (presence/absence indicator) rather than specific condition categories. Both source codes must be listed as unmapped.

memberDetails.text:
Think about all the vigorous activities that you did in the last 7 days. Vigorous physical activities refer to activities that take hard physical effort and make you breathe much harder than normal. Think only about those physical activities that you did for at least 10 minutes at a time.
 
 During the last 7 days, did you do vigorous physical activities like heavy lifting, digging, aerobics, or fast bicycling?

transforms.rationale: The source variable appears to be a binary Yes/No item (COPE_A_44=Yes, COPE_A_13=No) from a COPE instrument, which does not align with the TARGET CDE's frequency-based scale (No days through 6-7 days). There is no meaningful or confident mapping between a dichotomous Yes/No response and the ordinal day-count categories of the CDE. All source codes are left unmapped.

cde.id: Center for Epidemiologic Studies-Depression Scale (CES-D) - Restless sleep indicator

records.idealCde: Sleep Quality and Disturbance Assessment: A composite concept capturing the subjective quality, restlessness, and onset latency of sleep. Specifically addresses: (1) how often sleep was restless in the past week (ordinal frequency: rarely/none [<1 day], some/little [1-2 days], occasionally/moderate [3-4 days], all/most of the time [5-7 days]); (2) how often it took more than 30 minutes to fall asleep in the past month (ordinal frequency: never, less than once/week, once or twice/week, 3-5 times/week, 6-7 times/week); (3) duration of sleep-onset difficulty (decimal number, units in months or years as recorded); and (4) overall satisfaction with current sleep pattern (ordinal Likert scale: very satisfied to very dissatisfied). Member fields carry different time windows (past week vs. past month vs. unspecified duration) and different sleep dimensions (restlessness, onset latency, duration of complaint, overall satisfaction); these sub-dimensions should be retained as distinct items within the CDE rather than collapsed. Answer types are ordinal categorical scales for frequency and satisfaction items, and a decimal numeric with time units for duration.

transforms.rationale: Both scales measure sleep satisfaction along a 5-point continuum, so an ordinal rank-order mapping is applied: Very Satisfied→Very much, Satisfied→Quite a bit, Neutral→Somewhat, Dissatisfied→A little bit, Very Dissatisfied→Not at all. Confidence is moderate rather than high because the source scale is bipolar (satisfied↔dissatisfied) while the PROMIS scale is unipolar (degree of satisfaction only), so the negative end of the source (Dissatisfied/Very Dissatisfied) maps to low-satisfaction PROMIS codes rather than a true dissatisfaction construct, introducing conceptual imprecision.

records.concept: Lifetime diagnosis of anxiety disorder (doctor-told, ever)

cde.id: Psychiatric history clinical anxiety diagnosis indicator

records.idealCde: Anxiety disorder status and burden: A multi-faceted CDE capturing the presence, onset, current management, and recent symptom frequency of anxiety-related conditions (including anxiety reaction, panic disorder, phobia, and obsessive-compulsive disorder). Encompasses: (1) Lifetime diagnosis — whether a doctor has ever told the respondent they have an anxiety disorder (Yes/No); (2) Age at first diagnosis — life stage when first diagnosed (ordinal categories: Child [0–11], Adolescent [12–17], Adult [18–64], Older adult [65–74], Elderly [75+]); (3) Current treatment engagement — whether the respondent is still seeing a doctor or health care provider for anxiety/panic disorder (Yes/No); (4) Current medication/treatment — whether the respondent is currently prescribed medications or receiving treatment for anxiety/panic disorder (Yes/No); (5) Recent symptom frequency (past 2 weeks) — how often the respondent has been bothered by feeling nervous, anxious, or on edge (ordinal: Not at all / Several days / More than half the days / Nearly every day). All sub-elements pertain to the self-reporting participant. Answer types are categorical (nominal Yes/No for diagnosis and treatment items; ordinal life-stage categories for age at onset; ordinal frequency scale for symptom burden).

records.concept: Age at first diagnosis of anxiety reaction/panic disorder (ordinal life-stage categories)
records.idealCde: Anxiety disorder status and burden: A multi-faceted CDE capturing the presence, onset, current management, and recent symptom frequency of anxiety-related conditions (including anxiety reaction, panic disorder, phobia, and obsessive-compulsive disorder). Encompasses: (1) Lifetime diagnosis — whether a doctor has ever told the respondent they have an anxiety disorder (Yes/No); (2) Age at first diagnosis — life stage when first diagnosed (ordinal categories: Child [0–11], Adolescent [12–17], Adult [18–64], Older adult [65–74], Elderly [75+]); (3) Current treatment engagement — whether the respondent is still seeing a doctor or health care provider for anxiety/panic disorder (Yes/No); (4) Current medication/treatment — whether the respondent is currently prescribed medications or receiving treatment for anxiety/panic disorder (Yes/No); (5) Recent symptom frequency (past 2 weeks) — how often the respondent has been bothered by feeling nervous, anxious, or on edge (ordinal: Not at all / Several days / More than half the days / Nearly every day). All sub-elements pertain to the self-reporting participant. Answer types are categorical (nominal Yes/No for diagnosis and treatment items; ordinal life-stage categories for age at onset; ordinal frequency scale for symptom burden).

cde.id: Center for Epidemiologic Studies-Depression Scale (CES-D) - bother indicator

records.idealCde: Anxiety disorder status and burden: A multi-faceted CDE capturing the presence, onset, current management, and recent symptom frequency of anxiety-related conditions (including anxiety reaction, panic disorder, phobia, and obsessive-compulsive disorder). Encompasses: (1) Lifetime diagnosis — whether a doctor has ever told the respondent they have an anxiety disorder (Yes/No); (2) Age at first diagnosis — life stage when first diagnosed (ordinal categories: Child [0–11], Adolescent [12–17], Adult [18–64], Older adult [65–74], Elderly [75+]); (3) Current treatment engagement — whether the respondent is still seeing a doctor or health care provider for anxiety/panic disorder (Yes/No); (4) Current medication/treatment — whether the respondent is currently prescribed medications or receiving treatment for anxiety/panic disorder (Yes/No); (5) Recent symptom frequency (past 2 weeks) — how often the respondent has been bothered by feeling nervous, anxious, or on edge (ordinal: Not at all / Several days / More than half the days / Nearly every day). All sub-elements pertain to the self-reporting participant. Answer types are categorical (nominal Yes/No for diagnosis and treatment items; ordinal life-stage categories for age at onset; ordinal frequency scale for symptom burden).

records.concept: Perceived ease of finding equivalent employment elsewhere
records.idealCde: This source concept groups heterogeneous psychosocial and socioeconomic self-report items that do not share a single underlying construct; the member fields span at least five distinct measurement domains: (1) Perceived job mobility — the respondent's self-assessed ease of finding equivalent employment elsewhere, answered on a 3-point ordinal scale (Very easy / Somewhat easy / Not easy at all) plus Don't know / Prefer not to say / Not applicable; (2) Pre-retirement income adequacy expectation — the respondent's retrospective appraisal of whether household income and investments were expected to maintain their standard of living before retirement, answered on a 3-point ordinal scale (Adequate / Barely adequate / Inadequate); (3) Work- or school-based social network size — the count of people the respondent knows personally by name through work or school (excluding family, close friends, and neighbours), answered as a non-negative integer (count of persons); (4) Frequency of participation in educational and cultural activities involving others (e.g., courses, concerts, plays, museum visits) in the past 12 months, answered on a 6-point ordinal frequency scale (At least once a day / At least once a week / At least once a month / At least once a year / Never); (5) Lifetime and recent history of marital separation or divorce since age 16, answered as a 3-level categorical (No never / Yes but not in the last 12 months / Yes within the last 12 months) plus Prefer not to answer. Because these fields measure fundamentally different constructs, the ideal representation is five separate CDEs rather than one; if a single CDE must be chosen, it should be defined as a structured psychosocial profile instrument capturing employment mobility perception, retirement financial adequacy expectation, work/school social network size, cultural activity participation frequency, and marital disruption history, each as a distinct response element with its own answer type (ordinal categorical, ordinal categorical, integer count, ordinal frequency, and categorical lifetime/recent event respectively), all self-reported by the study participant with no laterality, body-site, or condition qualifier specified.

gencde.title: Perceived Ease of Finding Equivalent Employment Elsewhere
gencde.definition: A self-reported ordinal measure of how easy the respondent believes it would be to find a job with another employer offering approximately the same income and fringe benefits as their current position.
gencde.questionText: About how easy would it be for you to find a job with another employer with approximately the same income and fringe benefits you now have? Would you say very easy, somewhat easy, or not easy at all?

gencde.rationale: Source field AI-READI:pxji2 included sentinel codes 555 (Don't know), 777 (Prefer not to say), and 0 (Not applicable); only 'Prefer not to say' appeared in the reconciled ANSWER CONCEPTS list and is retained as a permissible value. 'Don't know' and 'Not applicable' were excluded per instructions to omit missing-data sentinels and concepts absent from the observed answer set. Codes were reassigned sequentially (1–3 for substantive responses, 7 for the administrative refusal option) to avoid confusion with the original sentinel numbering. The concept aligns with perceived external employability constructs in occupational psychology literature (e.g., Fugate et al., 2004) and is distinct from general health, quality of life, or vision-difficulty CDEs identified as near-misses.

gencde.rationale: Derived exclusively from CLSA variable RET_STDLIV_TRM. The three-point ordinal scale (Adequate / Barely adequate / Inadequate) is preserved as-is from the single observed source field; no additional permissible values were introduced. records.concept: Type of activity during periods of non-employment (gap coding)
records.idealCde: This source concept groups heterogeneous psychosocial and socioeconomic self-report items that do not share a single underlying construct; the member fields span at least five distinct measurement domains: (1) Perceived job mobility — the respondent's self-assessed ease of finding equivalent employment elsewhere, answered on a 3-point ordinal scale (Very easy / Somewhat easy / Not easy at all) plus Don't know / Prefer not to say / Not applicable; (2) Pre-retirement income adequacy expectation — the respondent's retrospective appraisal of whether household income and investments were expected to maintain their standard of living before retirement, answered on a 3-point ordinal scale (Adequate / Barely adequate / Inadequate); (3) Work- or school-based social network size — the count of people the respondent knows personally by name through work or school (excluding family, close friends, and neighbours), answered as a non-negative integer (count of persons); (4) Frequency of participation in educational and cultural activities involving others (e.g., courses, concerts, plays, museum visits) in the past 12 months, answered on a 6-point ordinal frequency scale (At least once a day / At least once a week / At least once a month / At least once a year / Never); (5) Lifetime and recent history of marital separation or divorce since age 16, answered as a 3-level categorical (No never / Yes but not in the last 12 months / Yes within the last 12 months) plus Prefer not to answer. Because these fields measure fundamentally different constructs, the ideal representation is five separate CDEs rather than one; if a single CDE must be chosen, it should be defined as a structured psychosocial profile instrument capturing employment mobility perception, retirement financial adequacy expectation, work/school social network size, cultural activity participation frequency, and marital disruption history, each as a distinct response element with its own answer type (ordinal categorical, ordinal categorical, integer count, ordinal frequency, and categorical lifetime/recent event respectively), all self-reported by the study participant with no laterality, body-site, or condition qualifier specified.

gencde.rationale: Source field is from UK Biobank (UKBB) gap coding module. Canonical permissible values were derived directly from observed answer concepts; missing-data sentinels (-121=Unknown cannot remember, -717=Other, -818=Prefer not to answer) were reconciled: 'Unknown, cannot remember' retained as a substantive response category (code 9); 'Prefer not to answer' was excluded as a missing-data sentinel per schema instructions; 'Other' retained as code 8. Codes are reassigned sequentially (1–9) replacing UKBB-specific numeric codes. The IDEAL CDE description indicated a heterogeneous concept spanning multiple domains; however, the single observed source field maps cleanly to a single categorical construct (gap activity type), so confidence is moderate rather than high. Near-miss CDEs (physical activity duration, job stop year, PART-O score) were used only to confirm non-overlap and inform alias vocabulary.

AoU:sdoh_intro.name: sdoh_intro
AoU:sdoh_intro.text:
Thank you (again) for being a part of the All of Us Research Program. Many things can make us sick or keep us healthy. Where you were born or where you live, go to school, or work can affect your health. These are sometimes referred to as social factors, or the "social determinants", of health. Help us learn more by completing this survey about your neighborhood, social life, stress, and feelings about your everyday life. This survey will take less than 10 minutes to complete.

Please answer each question as honestly as possible. It is important that you answer as many questions as you can. We are looking for your own answers, and not what you think your doctors, family, or friends want you to say.

Don't feel like you have to spend a long time on each question. The first answer that comes to you is usually the best one. If you aren't sure how to answer a question, choose the best answer from the options given. Some of the questions may be sensitive. You can choose not to answer.

  • GP surgery
  • Primary school
  • Post office
  • Public library
  • Leisure centre
  • NHS dentist
  • Secondary school
  • Transport nodes

UKBB:Degree to which abdominal pain/disc.name: Degree to which abdominal pain/discomfort/altered bowel habits affect/interfere with life in general
UKBB:Degree to which abdominal pain/disc.text:
Question asked: "Please indicate how much abdominal pain or discomfort or altered bowel habits are affecting or interfering with your life in general."

Participants were asked to move a slider to choose a number between 0 to 10, with 0 meaning "not at all" and 10 meaning "completely". Participants using an older browser were asked to select a button from 0 to 10.

The question in this field was taken from the IBS Severity Scoring System used with the authors' permission.

Francis CY, Morris J, Whorwell PJ. The irritable bowel severity scoring system: a simple method of monitoring irritable bowel syndrome and its progress. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics 1997;11(2):395-402

UKBB:Income score (England).name: Income score (England)
UKBB:Income score (England).text:
This domain measures the proportion of the population in an area experiencing deprivation related to low income. A combined count of income deprived individuals per LSOA is calculated by summing the following five indicators:
  • Adults and children in Income Support families
  • Adults and children in Income-Based Jobseeker's Allowance families
  • Adults and children in Pension Credit (Guarantee) families
  • Adults and children in Child Tax Credit families (who are not in receipt of Income Support, Income-Based Jobseeker's Allowance or Pension Credit) whose equivalised income (excluding housing benefits) is below 60 per cent of the median before housing costs
  • Asylum seekers in England in receipt of subsistence support, accommodation support, or both.

UKBB:Index of Multiple Deprivation (Engl.name: Index of Multiple Deprivation (England)
UKBB:Index of Multiple Deprivation (Engl.text:
The English Indices of Deprivation 2010 are measures of multiple deprivation at the small area level. The model of multiple deprivation which underpins the Indices of Deprivation 2010 is based on the idea of distinct domains of deprivation which can be recognised and measured separately. These domains are experienced by individuals living in an area. People may be counted in one or more of the domains, depending on the number of types of deprivation that they experience.

Each domain represents a specific form of deprivation experienced by people and each can be measured individually using a number of indicators. Seven distinct domains have been identified in the English Indices of Deprivation; Income Deprivation, Employment Deprivation, Health Deprivation and Disability, Education Skills and Training Deprivation, Barriers to Housing and Services, Living Environment Deprivation, and Crime. Individual domains can be used in isolation as measures of each specific form of deprivation. They can also be combined, using appropriate weights, into a single overall Index of Multiple Deprivation which can be used to rank every small area in England according to the deprivation experienced by the people living there. Along with two supplementary indices, Income Deprivation Affecting Children Index and Income Deprivation Affecting Older People Index, they form the English Indices of Deprivation. These statistics allow the most, and least, deprived areas of the country to be identified as well as providing information about the issues faced by people living in different parts of the country.

UKBB:Income score (Wales).name: Income score (Wales)
UKBB:Income score (Wales).text:
The purpose of this domain is to capture the extent of deprivation relating to income at a small area level across Wales. It focuses on the proportion of people living in households with income below a defined threshold or claiming benefits relating to low incomes. The indicators used for the income domain were:
  • Adults & children in income support households
  • Adults & children in pension credit households
  • Adults & children in income-based job seekers allowance households
  • Adults & children in tax credit (child tax credit and working tax credit) households below a low income threshold
  • National Asylum Support Service (NASS) supported asylum seekers in Wales in receipt of subsistence only and accommodation support

UKBB:Pulse wave peak to peak time.name: Pulse wave peak to peak time
UKBB:Pulse wave peak to peak time.text:
peak to peak time in milliseconds

A digital volume pulse can be considered to be the summation of a direct and a reflected component. The direct component is due to transmission of a pressure wave from the left ventricle to the finger via the most direct route. The reflected component is formed by pressure transmitted from the heart to the lower body where it is reflected back up the aorta and thence to the finger. peak to peak time is the difference between the peak values of direct and reflected components.

UKBB:Index of Multiple Deprivation (Wale.name: Index of Multiple Deprivation (Wales)
UKBB:Index of Multiple Deprivation (Wale.text:
The Welsh Index of Multiple Deprivation 2008 is the official measure of deprivation for small areas in Wales. It was developed for the Welsh Assembly Government by the Assembly's Statistical Directorate and the Local Government Data Unit (Wales).

The WIMD 2008 is made up of eight separate domains (or kinds) of deprivation: income, employment, health, education, housing, environment, access to services, and community safety.

Each of them was based on a range of different indicators which meant that they were measured in different ways using different units. So before they could be combined the measurements had to be transformed to make them compatible. For example, if the height of something had been measured in metres and the weight in kilograms it would not make sense simply to add them together.

Income and employment were classed as the most important factors, and they were given the biggest weighting in the overall index. Although there is more to deprivation than poverty, not having enough money or a job is a big part of it.

UKBB:Position of the pulse wave peak.name: Position of the pulse wave peak
UKBB:Position of the pulse wave peak.text:
position of the peak

A digital volume pulse can be considered to be the summation of a direct and a reflected component. The direct component is due to transmission of a pressure wave from the left ventricle to the finger via the most direct route. The reflected component is formed by pressure transmitted from the heart to the lower body where it is reflected back up the aorta and thence to the finger. This field is the time when the peak occurs in the waveform.

UKBB:Position of pulse wave notch.name: Position of pulse wave notch
UKBB:Position of pulse wave notch.text:
position of the notch

A digital volume pulse can be considered to be the summation of a direct and a reflected component. The direct component is due to transmission of a pressure wave from the left ventricle to the finger via the most direct route. The reflected component is formed by pressure transmitted from the heart to the lower body where it is reflected back up the aorta and thence to the finger. This is the time when when notch occurs in the waveform.

UKBB:Pulse wave pressure versus time res.name: Pulse wave pressure versus time response curve
UKBB:Pulse wave pressure versus time res.text:
Wave data containing 3 waveforms, each consisting of one direct and one reflected component.

A digital volume pulse can be considered to be the summation of a direct and a reflected component. The direct component is due to transmission of a pressure wave from the left ventricle to the finger via the most direct route. The reflected component is formed by pressure transmitted from the heart to the lower body where it is reflected back up the aorta and thence to the finger. Each waveform is actually a single pulse with 100 points. Since the heart rate is in beats per minute, a single beat takes 60seconds / Heart Rate and time between two beats is (60/Heart Rate)/100.

The data is formatted as follows:

  • The first number (i.e. digits before the first '|' character)indicate the number of points X,Y for the curve.
  • Each pair of X,Y values is separated by a '|' character from the preceding/succeeding pair.
  • Each pair of X,Y values is separated internally by a ',' character.
The X-axis is the time in milliseconds and the Y-axis is the Pulse signal strength in arbitrary units.

Purpose of Contact

Thank you (again) for being a part of the All of Us Research Program. Many things can make us sick or keep us healthy. Where you were born or where you live, go to school, or work can affect your health. These are sometimes referred to as social factors, or the "social determinants", of health. Help us learn more by completing this survey about your neighborhood, social life, stress, and feelings about your everyday life. This survey will take less than 10 minutes to complete.

Please answer each question as honestly as possible. It is important that you answer as many questions as you can. We are looking for your own answers, and not what you think your doctors, family, or friends want you to say.

Don't feel like you have to spend a long time on each question. The first answer that comes to you is usually the best one. If you aren't sure how to answer a question, choose the best answer from the options given. Some of the questions may be sensitive. You can choose not to answer.
